body_text: For decades, the keyboard was the physical extension of human thought. Today, a voice-first trend is bringing a new kind of productivity to our lives. The rhythmic clicking of keys has long been the drumbeat of the modern office. But as we move through 2026, another sound has joined the chorus. A softer, more conversational murmur. It’s the song of vibe coding, brainstorming, WhatsApp messaging and Slack chats. This change is not just a niche trend. After long years of promise, finally, voice is going mainstream. At least, according to The Wall Street Journal , there is a rising trend of office workers chatting to AI to dictate their messages which is “just a little awkward”. Awkward or not, it’s clear the knowledge workers are looking for other human ways to interact with the digital world, at work and in daily life. Makes more sense: adding speech to the sense of touch The keyboard has been our primary connection to the digital world for over a century. But even the best typists are limited by their fingers. Most of us type between 40 and 60 words per minute. Our thoughts move much faster than that. This is where speech comes in. We speak at a pace of 130 to 150 words per minute. Research from Stanford University shows that dictation is now three times faster than typing. It is also more accurate than ever. Modern AI tools now reach a 99% accuracy rate . Adding speech to your workflow does not mean throwing away your keyboard. It means using the right tool for the right task. Use your keys for data, editing long-form and precision. Use your voice away from your desk, for short-form messages, informal chats, drafting and brainstorming. This hybrid approach balances cognitive and physical effort. While skilled touch-typing is second nature, typing complex or long thoughts still introduces limits – it is slow. When you speak, that friction disappears. Dictation allows you to communicate your thoughts at the speed of conversation. This makes it perfect for brainstorming or rapid AI prompting. It is why doctors and lawyers have used dictation for years. Now, technology has made voice accessible for everyone. Instead of tediously drafting a 300-word AI prompt, you can spill it out in seconds, allowing AI to react to your intention as only AI can. In the same way, voice is a great way to brainstorm, with AI as your sparring partner. Logitech tools make for a smooth transition back and forth, from voice to keyboard to voice. The MX Keys S, for example, features a dedicated talk-to-text key. You do not have to change your habits to start speaking. You just tap a button and start talking. The popular Wispr Flow app does the same thing – push a button on any keyboard and you’re up and running. Or rather talking. Bottom line, at your desk, keyboards bring the power of your voice to your fingertips. Clear speech AI is only as accurate as the audio it receives. To master this trend, your desk tools must evolve. They need to prioritize audio clarity and easy integration. You need hardware for the voice revolution. Here is how the right setup transforms your experience: Logitech MX Keys S keyboard With this keyboard, you can switch between typing and speaking without breaking your focus. It has a dedicated button that opens your computer’s voice tool immediately. It helps you move quickly from entering data to dictating a summary, without losing your flow. Similarly, any keyboard can give you access to your computer’s native voice dictation or to an app like Wispr Flow or Willow Voice. You can even set up a shortcut through Logitech’s Options+ software. Logitech G Yeti GX mic or Logitech G Astro A50 X headset The Yeti GX is a specialist tool for the home office. It was originally built for elite streamers. It is a dynamic microphone with a supercardioid pickup pattern – a fancy way of saying it ignores background noise like air conditioners, chatter or traffic. It focuses only on your voice, giving your computer the clean audio it needs to transcribe your words accurately. Also, the Logitech G Astro A50 X headset is one of many gaming headsets that also feature similar software for voice clarity. Zone Wireless 2 headset Gone are the days of huddling close to a microphone to ensure only your voice is picked up. The Zone Wireless 2 headset uses AI to suppress background noise on both ends of your call – the perfect tool for a noisy office. While you talk, the smart microphones block out background noise. It also silences the room around you, letting you focus on your thoughts without being distracted by what’s happening nearby. Logitech MX Brio webcam If you work in a hybrid environment, the MX Brio is a powerful all-in-one choice. This webcam has microphones that stop the echo of your room from reaching the recording. You get high-quality video and clear voice capture from one device on your desk. Logitech MX Master 4 mouse Dictation is perfect for the first draft. Manual precision is better for the final edit. The MX Master 4 is the essential partner for this workflow. After you speak a long draft, this mouse is great for moving rapidly through long documents. Its quiet buttons mean you can make corrections without the microphone picking up the sound of your clicks. You can even use Logitech’s Options+ software to embed a Wispr Flow macro directly into one of its Action Ring’s dynamic on-screen “bubbles”, helping you engage your microphone instantly. A future we can touch and hear For over a century, we have expressed our thoughts through the reliable key. Today, we are moving away from a world where we only touch our technology. The keyboard did not replace the mouse. Nor will voice replace the keyboard. Each is just a powerful new partner for the other, working in symphony together. At the heart of all these input devices is a powerful truth – they help us extend our potential through our human senses. Touch, voice, hearing, sight. Each has its role and is incremental to the next. What is the first thing you’ll say to your computer today?

title: ADA Workplace Accommodations: How to Request Captioning Glasses From Your Employer
summary: 61% of workplace accommodations cost employers $0, and most of the rest stay under $300. Learn how to request captioning glasses under the ADA — what to write, what to attach, and how to win an appeal.
body_text: Editorial disclosure: AirCaps manufactures smart captioning glasses used by deaf and hard-of-hearing professionals across enterprise, healthcare, legal, and academic settings. This guide explains the ADA accommodation process generally and references our product alongside the broader landscape. Accommodation rules vary by employer, state, and circumstance — confirm specifics with your HR team, an EEOC counselor, or a disability rights attorney before filing. How Do You Request Captioning Glasses as an ADA Workplace Accommodation? You request captioning glasses as a reasonable accommodation by submitting a written request to your employer's HR or accessibility coordinator, attaching medical documentation of your hearing loss, and engaging in the ADA's required "interactive process." 61% of workplace accommodations cost employers $0 to implement, and the ones that do cost something carry a one-time median price of $300 ( Job Accommodation Network , 2025). At $599, captioning glasses fall within the typical accommodation budget — and the math gets easier when you compare a one-time hardware purchase to ongoing CART or interpreter services that run $100 to $290 per hour ( Karasch Captioning , 2024). The ADA's Title I provisions cover roughly 666,000 U.S. businesses with 15 or more employees, including most knowledge-work employers ( ADA National Network , 2024). If your employer falls in that group, they're legally required to consider your accommodation request — and the Job Accommodation Network's research shows 66% of employers rate the accommodations they implement as "very effective" or "extremely effective" ( JAN , 2025). This guide walks through the request process step by step: what to write, what to attach, how the interactive process works, and what to do if the answer is no. Key Takeaways 61% of workplace accommodations cost employers $0; the remaining 33% carry a one-time median cost of $300 — captioning glasses at $599 fit within the typical range ( JAN , 2025) The ADA covers employers with 15+ employees, reaching roughly 86 million U.S. workers across 666,000 businesses ( ADA National Network , 2024) 43.2% of EEOC merits suits filed in fiscal year 2024 contained ADA claims, and the agency filed 16 hearing-impairment cases across 2023-2024 — accommodation refusals are actively enforced ( EEOC Office of General Counsel , 2024) At a $150/hour CART rate, a $599 captioning glasses purchase pays for itself after roughly 4 hours of comparable service ( Karasch Captioning , 2024) Deaf adult employment hit a record 57.7% in 2024, but the gap to hearing peers still sits above 15 percentage points — meeting accessibility is the single biggest driver ( National Deaf Center , 2024) Table of Contents Does the ADA Actually Cover Captioning Glasses? What Does a Reasonable Accommodation Request Look Like? How Much Will Your Employer Actually Pay? Step-by-Step: The Interactive Process What Documents Should You Include? How to Write the Accommodation Request Letter What If Your Employer Says No? Captioning Glasses vs. CART, ASL, and Other Accommodations Frequently Asked Questions Does the ADA Actually Cover Captioning Glasses? Yes — captioning glasses qualify as auxiliary aids and services under the ADA when they enable an employee with hearing loss to perform essential job functions or participate in the workplace on equal terms with hearing peers. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission's published guidance specifically identifies "real-time captioning" and "assistive listening devices" as recognized accommodations for hearing-impaired employees ( EEOC Hearing Disabilities Guidance , 2024). Captioning glasses sit at the intersection of both categories — they show real-time text in your field of view while functioning as a wearable assistive device. The ADA's reasonable accommodation requirement applies to employers with 15 or more employees, which covers about 86 million U.S. workers across roughly 666,000 businesses ( ADA National Network , 2024). If your employer is in that group, they have a legal obligation to engage with your request — not necessarily to grant it, but to participate meaningfully in what the EEOC calls the "interactive process." A flat refusal without dialogue is itself an ADA violation. The legal landscape supports employees who pursue these claims. 43.2% of EEOC merits suits filed in fiscal year 2024 contained ADA claims, and the agency filed 42 disability-related lawsuits — nearly 40% more than in fiscal year 2022 ( EEOC Office of General Counsel , 2024). Among those, 16 cases over 2023 and 2024 specifically involved hearing-impaired employees. That doesn't mean every denial leads to a lawsuit, but it does mean enforcement is real and HR teams know it. There's a practical wrinkle worth knowing. The ADA doesn't require employers to provide the specific device the employee requests — it requires an effective accommodation. If your employer offers a different solution that genuinely works (a CART service, an FM system, or a real-time captioning app), that may satisfy the law. Your job is to make a clear case that captioning glasses are the most effective solution for your specific work pattern: hybrid meetings, hallway conversations, multi-speaker rooms, and the kinds of unscheduled interactions where booking a CART writer in advance isn't realistic. What Does a Reasonable Accommodation Request Look Like? A reasonable accommodation request is a written communication to your employer stating that you have a disability and need a specific change to perform your job. The EEOC's guidance is intentionally informal — there's no required form, no magic words, and no specific format. You don't even have to use the phrase "reasonable accommodation" or "ADA" ( EEOC Reasonable Accommodation Guidance , 2024). What you do need is enough information for your employer to recognize that you're requesting workplace support tied to a medical condition. A strong request includes four pieces: a statement that you have a disability, a description of how that disability affects your work, the specific accommodation you're proposing, and an offer to engage in the interactive process. You don't need to share your full medical history or even disclose the specific diagnosis — federal law lets you keep that private unless your employer has a genuine reason to ask for more. A simple "I have a documented hearing impairment that affects my participation in meetings and group conversations" is enough to trigger the employer's legal obligations. Citation Capsule: The EEOC's published guidance establishes that reasonable accommodation requests don't require specific forms, magic words, or even the term "ADA" — what matters is that the employee clearly conveys the existence of a medical condition and the need for workplace support ( EEOC , 2024). At that point, the employer's legal obligation to engage in the interactive process begins. Who do you send it to? In most companies, the right destination is your HR business partner or a designated accessibility coordinator. Smaller companies may not have a dedicated role — in that case, your direct manager or the senior-most HR contact works. Send the request by email so you have a written record, and ask for written acknowledgment when the request is received. The paper trail matters if the situation later escalates. One subtle point: you don't have to disclose your hearing loss to your manager or peers if you don't want to. The ADA gives you the right to confidential medical information, and your employer's HR team is legally required to keep your diagnosis private. You can have captioning glasses approved as an accommodation, wear them at work, and never explain why to your coworkers if you'd prefer the privacy. The AirCaps captioning glasses are designed for exactly this — under 2% light leakage means others can't see your captions, and the binocular display works behind any prescription lens. How Much Will Your Employer Actually Pay? Less than HR teams typically assume. The Job Accommodation Network's longitudinal employer survey — 1,425 respondents across 2019 through 2024 — found that 61% of accommodations cost employers nothing to implement. Of the remaining accommodations that did have a cost, 33% carried a one-time median price of $300, while only 6% involved an ongoing annual median cost of $2,400 ( JAN , 2025). At $599, AirCaps falls in the upper-third of typical one-time accommodation costs — well within what HR teams routinely approve without escalation. The comparison that wins approvals is the alternative cost. Industry pricing puts onsite CART captioning at $160 to $290 per hour, remote CART at $175 to $230 per hour, and onsite ASL interpretation at $100 to $220 per hour with a standard 2-hour minimum ( Karasch Captioning , 2024). A single all-day offsite with eight billable hours runs $1,500 to $3,000 before travel reimbursement. At a conservative $150 per hour blended rate, a $599 captioning glasses purchase pays for itself after roughly 4 hours of comparable CART service — meaning the return on investment lands inside the first week for any employee in regular meetings. CART and interpreter services require ongoing scheduling, vendor contracts, advance booking, and approval cycles. A captioning glasses purchase is a single procurement line, a single device, and zero ongoing operational overhead. For HR teams trying to keep their accommodation processes lightweight, the simplicity itself is a selling point. There's a separate question of whether your employer's insurance, health benefits, or HSA/FSA programs can offset the cost further. Many employers run flexible spending accounts that cover assistive devices — we cover the mechanics in our HSA and FSA guide for smart glasses . For our broader breakdown of insurance, Medicare, and benefits coverage, see our captioning glasses insurance guide . Step-by-Step: The Interactive Process The ADA requires employers to engage in what the EEOC calls "the interactive process" — a good-faith back-and-forth dialogue about your accommodation request. The process isn't optional. Skipping it or going through the motions without genuine consideration is itself a form of ADA violation. Here's how it typically unfolds, step by step. Step 1: Submit your written request to HR or the accessibility coordinator. Include a statement of your medical condition, a description of the workplace impact, the accommodation you're requesting (captioning glasses), and an offer to discuss alternatives. Keep your tone collaborative — this is a problem-solving conversation, not an adversarial filing. Step 2: Provide medical documentation if requested. Your employer can ask for verification that you have a disability and that the accommodation is medically appropriate, but they cannot ask for your full medical records or unrelated diagnoses. A Letter of Medical Necessity from your audiologist, ENT, or primary care physician is the standard document. It should state your diagnosis (in general terms — "documented hearing impairment" is enough), the workplace impact, and the recommended accommodation. Step 3: Participate in the interactive process meeting. Most employers will schedule a conversation with HR, your manager, and sometimes an outside accessibility consultant. The conversation should cover your essential job functions, the specific limitations your hearing loss creates, the proposed accommodation, and any alternatives the employer wants to explore. Bring documentation, but keep the tone solution-focused. Step 4: Receive the employer's decision in writing. Federal law doesn't set a strict deadline, but the EEOC expects responses to be timely — typically within 30 days for straightforward requests. The decision should be one of three options: approved as requested, approved with modification (a different but effective accommodation), or denied with a specific reason. Step 5: Implement and review. If approved, the employer purchases or reimburses the device, you start using it, and the team checks in periodically to confirm it's working. If problems arise — the device doesn't work as expected, the job changes, or new barriers emerge — the interactive process can reopen. Accommodations are living arrangements, not one-time transactions. Throughout the process, document everything. Save emails, take notes during meetings, and keep copies of every document you submit. If the situation escalates to an EEOC charge or lawsuit, the paper trail is your strongest evidence. The 16 hearing-impairment cases the EEOC filed in 2023 and 2024 typically turned on documentation gaps and procedural failures rather than disputes about whether the accommodation itself was reasonable. What Documents Should You Include? Five documents make the strongest accommodation request package. You don't need every one for every employer, but the more complete your initial submission, the faster the approval typically moves. The Letter of Medical Necessity is the foundation. Written by your audiologist, ENT, or primary care physician, it confirms your diagnosis and recommends captioning glasses as a medically appropriate accommodation. The ideal LMN includes your diagnosis (with the relevant ICD-10 code, typically H90 for sensorineural hearing loss), a description of how the condition affects communication, the recommended device, and the provider's credentials and signature. Most providers will write this during a standard appointment at no additional cost. A recent audiogram supports the LMN with measurable data. It shows your pure-tone air conduction thresholds, speech reception thresholds, and word recognition scores — particularly useful when accompanied by speech-in-noise testing that documents the exact problem captioning glasses solve. Reviewers who don't know much about hearing loss find the audiogram persuasive because it converts your experience into numbers and graphs. Document Where to Get It What It Proves Letter of Medical Necessity Audiologist, ENT, or PCP Device is medically required for diagnosed condition Recent Audiogram Audiologist (hearing test results) Severity and pattern of hearing loss Job Description and Essential Functions Your HR file or current job posting The communication-heavy duties the accommodation supports Product Specifications Manufacturer (AirCaps spec sheet) Technical capabilities and intended workplace use JAN Accommodation Guidance askjan.org topic pages Federally-funded recommendation of captioning technology The product specification sheet matters more than people expect. HR reviewers often have no working knowledge of captioning glasses, and they need a clear technical description to evaluate the request. Include the AirCaps specs: 4-microphone beamforming for noise rejection, 97% caption accuracy, 300ms latency, binocular MicroLED display with a 30-degree field of view, 49g weight, FCC and CE certifications, and HSA/FSA eligibility. Pulling these specs directly from manufacturer documentation positions the device as a serious assistive product rather than a consumer gadget. Reference the Job Accommodation Network's published guidance in your submission. JAN is funded by the U.S. Department of Labor and publishes detailed accommodation recommendations by disability type. Their hearing loss accommodation guidance specifically endorses speech-to-text and captioning technology, which makes the federal-government endorsement available to any HR team that doubts whether the request fits ADA norms. Citing JAN's guidance is one of the highest-leverage moves in an accommodation submission. Finally, a copy of your job description with essential functions highlighted helps connect the accommodation to your work. If you spend 60% of your time in meetings, that 60% needs accessible communication. If you do customer-facing presentations, the captioning supports your ability to handle Q&A. The connection between the accommodation and the job is what makes the request "reasonable" under the ADA — without that link, employers can argue the device isn't required for the role. How to Write the Accommodation Request Letter The accommodation request letter doesn't need to be long. A clear, well-structured one-page email beats a three-page filing every time. Use the template below as a starting point and adapt the language to your situation. Subject line: Reasonable Accommodation Request — [Your Name] Opening paragraph: State your purpose plainly. "I am writing to request a reasonable accommodation under the Americans with Disabilities Act. I have a documented hearing impairment that limits my ability to fully participate in meetings, group conversations, and other communication-intensive aspects of my role." Middle paragraphs: Describe the specific job impact and the requested accommodation. "In my current role as [job title], I attend an average of [X] meetings per week, many of which involve multiple speakers, fast-paced discussion, or hybrid in-person and remote participants. My hearing loss creates a meaningful barrier in these settings. I am requesting captioning glasses — specifically AirCaps, a $599 wearable device that displays real-time captions in my field of view — as the most effective accommodation for this work pattern." Cost and ROI paragraph: Address the business case directly. "AirCaps captioning glasses cost $599 as a one-time purchase, which falls within the typical workplace accommodation range — the Job Accommodation Network reports a one-time median cost of $300 for accommodations that have any cost, with 61% costing the employer nothing. Compared to CART captioning services at $160 to $290 per hour, the device pays back in roughly 4 hours of comparable use. I have attached a Letter of Medical Necessity from my audiologist, a recent audiogram, the AirCaps product specification sheet, and JAN's hearing loss accommodation guidance." Closing paragraph: Invite the interactive process. "I am happy to discuss alternative accommodations if you believe a different solution would be more effective, and I welcome the opportunity to participate in the interactive process. Please let me know what additional information you need and when we can schedule a conversation. I am available [your availability]." A few tone notes. Keep the language professional but warm — you're asking for support, not threatening litigation. Avoid words like "demand" or "require" in the early stages; the law uses "request" and so should you. Reference the ADA explicitly once, in the opening paragraph, so the legal context is clear without belaboring it. If your relationship with HR is good, you can lean toward conversational; if your employer has a track record of denying accommodations, lean toward formal and complete documentation from the start. Send the letter by email and keep the read receipt. Ask for written acknowledgment within five business days. If you don't hear back, follow up in writing — silence is not an acceptable response under the ADA, and federal courts have consistently treated employer non-response as evidence of bad-faith engagement. What If Your Employer Says No? The first denial usually isn't really a denial — it's a request for more information or a counter-offer. Read the denial carefully and identify which of the three common patterns applies: outright refusal, alternative-accommodation proposal, or "we need more documentation" delay. Each pattern has a different response strategy. Pattern 1: The employer proposes a different accommodation. This is the most common outcome — your employer may suggest a CART service, an FM system, an iPhone captioning app, or moving you to a quieter workspace. The ADA permits this as long as the alternative is genuinely effective. Your job is to evaluate the alternative honestly. If it works for your job pattern, accept it. If it doesn't — say, CART that requires advance booking when most of your meetings are impromptu — explain specifically why the proposed alternative fails and re-propose captioning glasses with the gap clearly defined. Pattern 2: The employer asks for more documentation. This often means the medical documentation didn't establish a clear connection between your condition and the workplace impact. Respond with a stronger Letter of Medical Necessity that explicitly addresses the job functions, an audiogram with speech-in-noise testing if you don't have one, and references to JAN's hearing loss accommodation guidance. Documentation requests are usually not bad-faith — HR teams want defensible paperwork in case the request is audited. Pattern 3: The employer denies the request outright on "undue hardship" grounds. "Undue hardship" is the only legal exception to ADA accommodations, but it's a high bar. The EEOC defines undue hardship as significant difficulty or expense — not minor inconvenience. A $599 one-time purchase almost never qualifies, but employers occasionally cite undue hardship for accommodations they don't want to provide. If you receive an undue hardship denial, request the specific financial or operational evidence the employer relied on, and consider escalating. Escalation has three steps. First, request an internal appeal through your HR department or accessibility office. Most companies have a formal review process — use it. Second, file a charge of discrimination with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission within 180 days of the denial. EEOC charges are free, you don't need a lawyer, and the agency will investigate. The EEOC's enforcement record matters here — 43.2% of merits suits filed in fiscal year 2024 contained ADA claims, and disability cases consistently make up one of the agency's top enforcement categories ( EEOC , 2024). Third, consult a disability rights attorney. The National Association of the Deaf, the Disability Rights Education and Defense Fund, and your state's Protection and Advocacy agency all maintain referral networks. Many disability attorneys take ADA cases on a contingency basis — meaning you don't pay unless you win. The legal community treats accommodation denials as serious cases, and a well-documented denial often resolves at the demand letter stage without going to court. One realistic note: most accommodation requests don't reach this level of conflict. The vast majority of HR teams approve reasonable requests once they understand the cost, the technology, and the legal context. The escalation path exists because some employers do refuse — but the average reader of this guide will probably never need to use it. Captioning Glasses vs. CART, ASL, and Other Accommodations The honest comparison: captioning glasses don't replace every hearing accommodation, and they're not always the right choice. The best accommodation for your situation depends on your specific work pattern, your communication preferences, and the kinds of meetings you actually attend. Here's how to think about the trade-offs. CART (Communication Access Realtime Translation) remains the gold standard for formal events — board meetings, court proceedings, conferences, and any setting where verbatim accuracy is legally or professionally critical. A human captioner reaches near-perfect accuracy and handles specialized vocabulary, proper names, and acronyms better than any current AI system. The downside is cost and scheduling — CART writers book days in advance and charge $100 to $290 per hour. For employees who can plan around scheduled events, CART is excellent. For employees whose work depends on unscheduled hallway conversations, it's not workable as a daily solution. ASL interpretation is the right accommodation for ASL-fluent deaf professionals, particularly in settings where conceptual nuance, two-way conversation, and cultural fluency matter. ASL interpreters can also relay tone, emotion, and context that text-based captioning misses. The downsides parallel CART — interpreters book in advance, cost $100 to $220 per hour, and require two-hour minimums. ASL is also irrelevant for hard-of-hearing employees who don't sign, which is a large share of the deaf and hard-of-hearing professional population. Auto-captioning meeting apps (Otter, Google Meet captions, Zoom live transcripts) work well for video meetings but break down in person. They require a laptop or phone, they typically don't filter background noise, and they force the user to look at a screen instead of the speaker. For employees whose meetings are 100% remote, they're often sufficient. For hybrid or in-person work, they leave a major gap. FM systems and hearing loops amplify sound directly to a hearing aid or cochlear implant. They work brilliantly for fixed locations with installed infrastructure — many universities, theaters, and large conference rooms have them. The limitations are portability (you can't bring a hearing loop to a coffee meeting) and applicability (they help only if you wear compatible hearing aids). Captioning glasses fill the gap that other accommodations leave open: ambient, in-person, multi-speaker, unscheduled conversations. Our AirCaps captioning glasses deliver 97% accuracy at 300ms latency through 4-microphone beamforming, identify up to 15 different speakers in real time, and support 60+ languages with automatic detection — useful for multilingual workplace settings and international business calls. The AirCaps meeting intelligence layer adds automated summaries, action item extraction, and searchable conversation history that complement the live captions. None of these features replace CART for a formal board meeting, but they cover the 80% of communication that happens outside scheduled formal events. The optimal accommodation stack for most deaf and hard-of-hearing professionals is layered: captioning glasses for daily ambient use, CART for high-stakes formal events, and auto-captioning apps as a backup for routine video meetings. You don't have to pick one — and the ADA's interactive process is the right venue to negotiate a stack that actually fits your work. Frequently Asked Questions Can my employer refuse to pay for captioning glasses if they cost too much? Only if the cost would create "undue hardship" — a high legal standard requiring significant difficulty or expense. At $599, captioning glasses fall within the typical workplace accommodation range, with 61% of accommodations costing $0 and the rest carrying a median cost of $300 ( JAN , 2025). For most U.S. employers covered by ADA Title I, $599 doesn't meet the undue hardship threshold — particularly when compared to ongoing CART or interpreter costs. Do I have to disclose my specific diagnosis to HR? No. The ADA gives you the right to confidentiality around your specific medical condition. You need to confirm that you have a disability and that the accommodation is medically appropriate, but you don't have to disclose the underlying diagnosis to your manager, your peers, or anyone other than the HR or accessibility coordinator who reviews your request. Federal law requires HR teams to keep medical information confidential. What if I work remotely — does the ADA still apply? Yes. The ADA applies to remote workers the same way it applies to in-person workers, and the Bureau of Labor Statistics reports that 25% of disabled workers worked from home in some capacity in 2024 ( BLS , 2024). Remote work often actually strengthens the case for captioning glasses, which work equally well in video meetings, hybrid setups, and in-person sessions — unlike CART or interpreter services that require scheduled bookings. How long does the accommodation request process take? The EEOC expects employers to respond promptly, but federal law doesn't set a strict deadline. Most straightforward requests resolve within 30 days. Requests that involve documentation gaps, alternative accommodation proposals, or formal interactive process meetings can take 60 to 90 days. If your employer is taking longer than 90 days without a substantive response, you can file an EEOC charge or request an internal escalation. Can I use my HSA or FSA if my employer denies the accommodation? Yes. HSA and FSA accounts let you pay for captioning glasses with pre-tax dollars regardless of whether your employer formally accommodates the device. IRS Publication 502 lists hearing aids and assistive communication equipment as qualified medical expenses, and AirCaps is HSA/FSA eligible. We cover the mechanics in our HSA and FSA guide for smart glasses . Does my employer have to provide my exact device of choice? Not necessarily. The ADA requires an "effective" accommodation, not necessarily your preferred one. If your employer offers a different solution that genuinely works for your job pattern, that may satisfy the law. Your strongest case for the specific device you want is to demonstrate why alternatives don't work — typically through documentation of the unscheduled, multi-speaker, ambient communication settings that other accommodations can't cover. Start Your Accommodation Request Today Here's the practical sequence: schedule an audiologist or ENT appointment to update your audiogram and obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity, gather the AirCaps product specification sheet and the JAN hearing loss accommodation guidance, draft a one-page request letter using the template above, and send it to your HR business partner or accessibility coordinator by email. Most requests resolve within 30 days, and HR teams overwhelmingly approve well-documented accommodation submissions for devices in the $599 range. AirCaps captioning glasses weigh 49 grams, deliver 97% caption accuracy at 300ms latency through 4-microphone beamforming, and display real-time captions on a binocular MicroLED waveguide with under 2% light leakage — invisible to colleagues across the table. The device supports 60+ languages with automatic detection, identifies up to 15 speakers, and works with any prescription from minus 16 to plus 16 diopters via interchangeable lens holders. Every specification supports the medical-device classification that makes ADA accommodation requests defensible. The ADA exists because workplace accessibility is a civil right, not a favor. The interactive process is your legal entitlement, not a special accommodation your employer is doing you. Most HR teams know this — and the ones that don't usually figure it out when they see the documentation. Ask in their language, attach the right paperwork, and the approval typically follows. title: The 5 Types of ERP Integration — and What Each One Reveals About Your Architecture
summary: The five types of ERP integration each signal a gap in your ERP architecture. Composable, headless ERP architecture eliminates most of them.
body_text: Want to test drive the most customizable ERP platform in the market? The types of ERP integration your business relies on are a diagnostic signal. Each one represents something your ERP wasn’t meant to do natively — a gap where you found a workaround. The more integrations your ERP requires, the more your architecture is patching over gaps that your core system wasn’t built to handle. With a better architecture, you don’t need all these integrations. This blog post covers the five most common ERP integration types, what each one reveals about your system, and what a better architectural foundation looks like. What You’ll Learn 5 ERP integration types and their architecture red flags What your integration map is really telling you How composable, headless architecture eliminates most of these integration types Choosing the right ERP integration approach for where you are now 5 ERP Integration Types and Their Architecture Red Flags Each of the following integration types exists because of something your ERP wasn’t built to do natively. Here’s what each one is, why you might use it, and what it shows about your architecture. #1. Point-to-Point Integration With point-to-point integration, two systems are wired together directly, one pair at a time. This is a common integration approach, but also highly fragile. What it is: A direct API or file-based connection between two specific systems. Why teams use it: It’s fast to set up, with no need for a middleware layer. What it reveals: Since your ERP doesn’t natively share data models, every new system requires a new manual connection. The real cost: Point-to-point is brittle and unable to scale, with each connection being a maintenance liability. #2. ESB and Middleware Integration ESBs and middleware are intended to manage the chaos of point-to-point. But in doing so, they bring a new layer of complexity. What it is: A central messaging layer that routes data between systems. Why teams use it: It reduces direct dependencies between systems and allows for some standardization. What it reveals: Your ERP is not the authoritative source of truth. It needs a translation layer to communicate with the rest of your tools. The real cost: Implementation is heavy and calls for specialized expertise. Plus, the middleware itself often becomes a bottleneck. #3. iPaaS Integration iPaaS cloud-native platforms like MuleSoft, Boomi, and Workato make integrations more accessible. But they don’t change the underlying architectural problem. You’re still building around your ERP’s limitations. What it is: Cloud-based integration platforms with pre-built connectors and low-code workflows. Why teams use it: It’s faster to build and easier to maintain and scale than ESB. What it reveals: Your ERP still can’t natively communicate with the tools your business actually runs on. The real cost: Ongoing licensing fees; vendor lock-in; and integration maintenance for every workflow change. #4. Custom and Bespoke Integration When you can’t get what you need from middleware or iPaaS, teams write custom code. This works up to a point, but breaks down when something changes and requires extensive documentation to perform maintenance successfully. What it is: Internally-built connectors, scripts, or microservices that handle specific data flows. Why teams use it: Teams build custom ERP integrations to handle unique business logic, unsupported edge cases, or legacy system constraints. What it reveals: Your ERP’s data model or process logic don’t map to how your business actually works. The real cost: Ongoing engineering ownership and a risk every time a connected system updates. #5. Direct Database Integration Bypassing the application layer and going right to the database is a last resort — a signal that every other option has failed. What it is: Reading from or writing directly to an ERP’s underlying database (outside of any API layer). Why teams use it: API limitations, performance requirements, or having no other option. What it reveals: The ERP’s application layer is too rigid for what the business needs. The real cost: Direct database integrations are highly fragile, often break during upgrades, and tend to be undocumented or poorly maintained. What Your Integration Map Is Really Telling You When you view your integrations as a collective picture rather than separate projects, a pattern will start to appear. If you’re dealing with integration sprawl, this is a sign that your ERP is functioning as a rigid core the rest of the business has to work around. Look for these signals that your ERP architecture is working against you: You’re maintaining more connectors than core ERP workflows. Every new business process requires a new integration project. Your engineering team spends more time on integration maintenance than on building new capability. System upgrades get delayed or avoided because they always break something. You choose new tools based on whether they’ll work with your ERP (not on whether they’re actually the best fit). Onboarding a new system takes months because of all the integration work required. When a connector breaks, no one knows who owns it. These aren’t integration problems. They’re architecture problems. And that means they have an architectural solution. How Composable, Headless Architecture Eliminates Most of These Integration Types A composable business architecture takes the best tools and unifies them. A composable ERP is modular by design, letting you swap individual components without rebuilding core operations. It’s API-first and built around a flexible data model you control. Composable architecture gives you a foundation where most connectors aren’t needed. Instead of a rigid system you’re forced to integrate around, you have a platform you compose with. With A Traditional ERP With Composable, Headless ERP Every new system needs a custom connection Systems share a common data model natively Middleware is required just to route data Clean APIs make middleware optional, not mandatory Unique business logic gets hardcoded into connectors Logic lives in the platform, not in bespoke scripts Direct database access fills the gaps your API can’t Proper APIs expose what you need Upgrades make integrations break The modular design means changes stay contained Your integration map shrinks because your architecture is doing the job it’s supposed to. Tailor is built headless and composable, designed specifically for the operational complexity that traditional ERPs force you to integrate around. With a unified backend and a decoupled frontend interface, your system speaks the same language as your entire stack, without the connectors holding it together. Choosing the Right ERP Integration Approach for Where You Are Now The “best” type of ERP integration depends on where your business is right now and how much technical debt you’re comfortable taking forward. Use iPaaS when: You need to move quickly, you have a modern ERP with solid APIs, and you’re okay with the ongoing licensing cost. Use middleware/ESB when: You’re a large enterprise with heavy governance requirements and existing infrastructure to handle this approach. Build custom when: You have truly unique business logic that no platform supports, and you have the engineering capacity to own and maintain it. Choose composable architecture when: You’re scaling fast, your business model is changing, and integration debt is slowing your growth. The first three approaches are best used in the specific circumstances listed. But if you’ve been cycling through all three of them, this is a sign your architecture needs to change. Tailor is designed to support teams in this exact situation. [Book a demo to see how a composable, headless ERP handles complexity](https://www.tailor.tech/demo, eliminating connectors and enabling you to scale.

title: My Path into Mainframe: A Second Start That Stuck
summary: Read how Amarildo Golloshi’s second chance in Broadcom’s Vitality Residency Program helped him build a lasting career in mainframe.
body_text: The call didn’t feel real at first. After everything it took just to get to that point, hearing that I had been accepted into Broadcom’s Vitality Residency Program wasn’t just good news, it was validation of persistence through uncertainty. Because my path into technology wasn’t a straight line. And my path into the mainframe was even less so. How Programming Challenges Sparked Curiosity Like many people in tech, my interest began early. In high school, I was introduced to programming, and it immediately clicked. Not because it was easy, but because it wasn’t. Every assignment felt like a problem waiting to be solved, and I enjoyed the process of figuring it out. That curiosity carried into college, where I pursued Computer Science. Over time, what started as interest became something more intentional. I began to understand not just how code works, but why it matters. The ability to build something from nothing, solve real problems, create impact really stuck with me. From Building Code, to Teaching Code After graduating, I stepped into a software development role. It was the first time everything I had learned became tangible. Writing production code, debugging issues, working with a team, all felt like forward momentum. Then something unexpected happened. I was offered a part-time role teaching programming. That experience changed how I think about technology. Teaching forced me to slow down and truly understand what I knew. Explaining complex ideas simply is harder than writing the code itself. It sharpened my communication, strengthened my fundamentals, and gave me a new appreciation for mentorship. It also taught me how important structured learning environments are, something I would later value even more. Resetting My IT Career Then came the reset. I moved to the United States with the goal of continuing my career in IT. What I didn’t fully anticipate was how much of a restart that would require. New market, no network, and a level of competition that made it difficult to get traction. For a while, progress felt stalled. I kept learning, kept applying, kept adjusting. Eventually, I found LaunchCode, which introduced me to something I hadn’t seriously considered before: mainframe technology. The Miss That Mattered I applied to the Vitality Residency Program once and didn’t get in. That could have been the end of the story. At that point, I had already turned down other opportunities because I was focused on building a long-term path in technology. There was real pressure to pivot, to choose something more immediate and stable. But I applied again because I wasn’t ready to give up on the direction I believed in. And when I was accepted the second time around, I didn’t come in as an expert. I came in curious and prepared to learn. Entering the Mainframe World Before the program started, I spent time in IBM Z Xplore just getting familiar with the environment. Once the program began, the pace accelerated quickly. In the first several weeks, I was introduced to the core of mainframe systems programming: z/OS, ISPF, JCL, SDSF, REXX, and COBOL. To me, these tools represented a different way of thinking about computing. Stability, scale, and precision mattered in a way that felt distinct from other environments I had worked in. From there, I trained on Broadcom’s Top Secret security product, adding another layer of depth to what I was learning. And then came the transition from training to doing. From Learning to Contributing After six months, I moved into my residency as a systems programmer, and that’s where everything connected. The systems I work on now aren’t theoretical. They support real business operations at scale. The margin for error is smaller, but the impact is larger. Every task requires attention, discipline, and continuous learning. What stood out to me most wasn’t just the technology. It was the structure around it. The program didn’t just teach tools; it built confidence through repetition, mentorship, and real-world application. That combination is what made the difference. What This Path Actually Taught Me There’s a common idea that success is about momentum. That once things start moving, they keep moving. That wasn’t my experience. Throughout my IT journey, progress came in phases. Periods of growth, followed by setbacks. Moments of clarity, followed by doubt. The difference wasn’t avoiding those cycles, it was continuing through them. Rejection wasn’t the opposite of progress. In my case, it was part of it. Finding a Sustainable Career Direction Choosing this path, especially the second time, required patience. It required saying no to short-term options in favor of something less certain but more aligned with where I wanted to go. The Vitality Residency Program didn’t just give me a role. It gave me a direction that feels sustainable. And the mainframe–something I hadn’t initially planned for–turned out to be exactly the kind of environment where I could grow long-term. Following the Path of Persistence If there’s one thing I would pass on, it’s this: The path doesn’t need to be obvious to be the right one. Sometimes the opportunities that stick are the ones you almost walked away from. Believe in yourself, even when the path seems unclear, because persistence will always open doors that talent alone cannot. LEARN MORE About the Author About the Author Amarildo Golloshi

title: Statement Pieces: How to Make Your Space Unforgettable

body_text: Your home should tell a sto­ry. Not a qui­et one, but a bold, inter­est­ing sto­ry that makes peo­ple stop and say, “ where did you find that? ” That’s the pow­er of a state­ment piece. State­ment pieces are con­ver­sa­tion starters. They trans­form a room from “nice” to “wow.” And the best part? They don’t have to cost a fortune. What Makes a Statement Piece? OK, let’s start with the basics. What the heck is a state­ment piece any­way, and who decides what makes the cut? While style might be sub­jec­tive, we can all agree that fur­ni­ture (or art) that com­mands atten­tion or evokes sur­prise is what a state­ment piece is all about. Here are a few examples. Unapolo­get­i­cal­ly bold in col­or. Think emer­ald green vel­vet sofa or a sun­shine yel­low credenza. Dis­tinc­tive in shape. Such as a sculp­tur­al accent chair, a sun­burst mir­ror, or a geo­met­ric cof­fee table. Unique­ly designed. This could be a vin­tage find, mid-cen­tu­ry clas­sic, or hand-made piece with real character Lay­ered in tex­ture. Try a woven wall hang­ing, a rat­tan book­shelf, or a brass-legged din­ing table. Pure visu­al inter­est. Abstract wall art, a pat­terned accent wall, or a show-stop­ping light­ing fixture. What do they have in com­mon? They make a room feel inten­tion­al and personal. Why Go Bold? Play­ing it safe might be eas­i­er. But it’s also for­get­table. Com­mit­ting to just one or two state­ment pieces in a room can embold­en you and ground your space in your per­son­al­i­ty. Here’s what happens: Your space feels more “you” A bold choice is an act of self-expres­sion. It says you have taste, you’re con­fi­dent in your style, and you’re not afraid to take a cre­ative risk. Your home becomes a reflec­tion of who you are, not a cat­a­log page. (Remem­ber Phoebe and Rachel’s apothe­cary table?) One piece sets the tone for everything A great state­ment piece anchors a room. Once you have it, build­ing the rest of your décor becomes eas­i­er. Col­ors, tex­tures, and oth­er pieces nat­u­ral­ly fall into place around it. It’s a conversation starter Friends notice and ask ques­tions. Your space becomes a back­drop for sto­ries, which is part of the mag­ic of bold design. It’s going to make you want to throw par­ties so more peo­ple will see it. (No, seriously.) You can save money on quality Here’s the sec­ond­hand secret: a stun­ning mid-cen­tu­ry cre­den­za or design­er chair that is pre-loved costs a frac­tion of the new retail price. Your room looks high-end like an Insta­gram show­room, but with­out the high-end price tag. How to Style Statement Pieces Like a Pro Resist the urge to sur­round your state­ment piece with oth­er bold ele­ments, giv­ing it some space to shine. Pair a dra­mat­ic sofa with neu­tral walls and a sim­ple area rug. Hang strik­ing wall art with plen­ty of white space around it. The min­i­mal­ism makes the bold­ness even more powerful. Pull col­ors or tex­tures from your state­ment piece into small­er décor items. If you have a jew­el-tone vel­vet chair, echo that col­or in throw pil­lows or a piece of art. If you have a tex­tured wood cre­den­za, repeat that warmth in a wood­en mir­ror frame or shelv­ing. These con­nec­tions cre­ate harmony. Shop­ping vin­tage is a great way to intro­duce a state­ment piece. They’re one-of-a-kind and already car­ry his­to­ry. Pair a vin­tage state­ment chair with mod­ern side tables. Mix a sculp­tur­al brass lamp with min­i­mal­ist wall shelves. This con­trast keeps spaces from feel­ing dat­ed or over­ly themed. Pro tip: One state­ment piece does­n’t have to be fur­ni­ture. A strik­ing piece of wall art, an over­sized mir­ror, or a sculp­tur­al floor lamp can anchor a space just as effec­tive­ly as a sofa or cre­den­za. Think beyond tra­di­tion­al furniture. You can dis­cov­er design­er finds and one-of-a-kind vintage. You’re being sus­tain­able and giv­ing qual­i­ty fur­ni­ture a sec­ond life. You get white-glove deliv­ery and assem­bly, even for the largest state­ment pieces. A stun­ning vin­tage cre­den­za or design­er accent chair becomes acces­si­ble. That’s the Apt­De­co difference. title: Zoom on Zoom: how Marketing Remix was built on Zoom Events (2026)

body_text: Watch the event that inspired this playbook Watch on demand Marketing Remix is Zoom's inaugural virtual marketing event designed to spark conversation, and create real community among marketing professionals. In 2026, we ran it across five regions: North America, EMEA, Japan, APAC, and Korea, with regionalized sessions designed for each audience. Every piece of it, from the first registration email to the post event follow-up, ran inside one platform. That platform was Zoom Events. Here's how we built it and what we learned. Zoom Events is an all-in-one virtual event platform that lets teams plan, host, and extend multi-session virtual events from registration through post-event AI content generation, without managing a stack of separate tools. We know because we built our own event on it. Marketing Remix combined pre-recorded sessions, a live host threading everything together and engaging with the audience in real time, and a fully live cameras on after-party, all inside one platform. Registration, email, backstage coordination, scene transitions, analytics, and follow-up content all in one tool. All of it on Zoom. Here's the playbook. How we built a virtual event without the chaos Pre-event is where most programs bleed time. Speaker list in one place, registration page in another, promo calendar somewhere else, email platform who-knows-where. Here's how we used Zoom Events to pull it all into one place, saving valuable time, and what we learned about how to run a virtual event when the clock was ticking. We built the registration hub in one place . Because Zoom Events provides custom registration pages, speaker bios, session scheduling, and registration management from a single dashboard, when speaker schedules shifted late in our planning cycle, we were able to update the backend and reshuffle sessions in minutes, not hours, and without a developer request and CMS update. Instead, it was just a few clicks. See planning and hosting virtual events for a full walkthrough. Our session format was a deliberate choice . Marketing Remix wasn't just a webinar with a twist. Pre-recorded sessions gave us polish and the flexibility to feature speakers across multiple time zones and tailor content for regional audiences. Our event host, Josh Brage, customer enablement specialist at Zoom, joined live as the connective thread between segments. That was a deliberate strategy: with Josh live, he could react to the chat in real time, respond to audience energy, and create genuine moments of human connection that pre-recorded content alone can't replicate. A fully live after-party promoting 2-way dialog between speakers and attendees for real connection and community, complete with a DJ closed the event. Zoom Events handles simulive and fully live sessions simultaneously, with no mode switch and no tool swap. That wasn't a workaround. It was the plan. We designed our email cadence around how people actually register . Registration is front-loaded. Most conversions from any given email happen in the first 48 hours, not spread across the following week. A denser cadence beats a slow drip. And because our email tools lived inside the same platform as the event, we could see registration velocity in real time and adjust without exporting a single thing. Our speakers carried some of the heavy lifting . One of the most successful pre-event promotions we ran came from the people already on our agenda. LinkedIn content from confirmed speakers reached an audience that already trusts the source. Zoom Events tracks registration by source, so we could see what was working and do more of it. How Zoom Events performed during the live event See every Zoom Webinar and Events feature Explore Zoom solutions Four things defined how Marketing Remix ran on the day. Backstage as our green room. The audience never sees it. We used Backstage to keep Josh synced between segments, giving him real-time visibility into live chat activity and active Q&A threads so he could stay present and responsive with the audience throughout the show. For a format where pre-recorded precision had to feel seamlessly connected by a live host, Backstage is what made that possible. Simulive and live sessions let us pair polished pre-recorded content with Josh's live presence and a fully live afterparty, all in the same event, handled by the platform. Pre-recorded sessions delivered the precision. Josh and the afterparty delivered the energy. Attendees got both, and we never had to manage them as separate productions. Real-time engagement tools — Q&A, reactions, and chat — serve two purposes: they give attendees a reason to stay active, and they generate the behavioral data that makes post-event follow-up useful. Marketing Remix exceeded attendance goals by 16%, achieving a registration rate that outpaced our prior event benchmarks. That number was in the dashboard the moment the event closed. Gamification turned participation into a moment . One of the highest-engagement spikes of the event wasn't a session — it was the Battle of the Band Names. We asked attendees to drop their best marketing-themed band name in the chat, and the response was immediate: "Panic at the Breakout Room." "The Bottom Funnel Boys." "Can You See My Screen." "Me, Myself, and AI." Dozens of entries flooded in across all regions. Beyond the energy it created, it demonstrated something our own webinar research backs up: well-timed, low-friction participation prompts are one of the most effective levers for spiking engagement, especially during natural lulls. We applied the same logic to polls throughout the event, using them not just as data collection, but as deliberate reset points to re-engage attention between segments. Production Studio handled branded overlays, lower thirds, and transitions natively: broadcast-quality visuals without a production agency, and without a second operator. For an event running live across five regions, that consistency mattered. One person, one platform, professional output at every session. How Zoom analytics and post-event insights drove pipeline Most teams walk out of a virtual event with two files: a registrant list and an attendee list. Every question asked, every session attended, every reaction fired, all flattened into a spreadsheet with no context attached. We've been on the other side of that handoff. It's not great. Post-event, the team used the platform's analytics dashboard and AI Content Generation feature to segment attendees by topic interest and generate personalized follow-up content, without standing up any additional infrastructure. The Summary tab gave us three numbers immediately: registration rate, live attendance rate, and a composite engagement score from 0 to 10, benchmarked against our full event history. We knew within minutes whether the event over- or underperformed and exactly which metric moved. The Engagement tab gave us individual attendee profiles: time on session, questions asked, topics of interest auto-tagged from Q&A language. That context is what made follow-up land. An attendee who stayed 40 minutes and asked pointed questions about a specific topic gets routed to the SDR team with that signal attached, not dropped into a generic sequence. AI Content Generation took that data further. It combed session transcripts, cross-referenced attendee engagement, and automatically created follow-up email drafts segmented by topic interest. The team can review and polish content before sending,, but the lift of writing individualized emails from scratch was gone. For more on connecting event performance to pipeline, see measuring webinar ROI and impact . The value of that signal became clear in the event itself. In the Metadata session, James Silvestri shared that 23% of their closed deals were influenced by virtual events, with a close rate 2.5x higher than other channels, a result that starts with capturing the right behavioral data in the platform. Example numbers of how analytics are displayed How we repurposed our webinar content after Marketing Remix The live energy faded, but the recordings, transcripts, and clips inside Zoom Events didn't. We matched the content format to what the live sessions delivered. Data-heavy sessions translated well into written content: blog posts, how-to guides, and structured articles. Conversations and panel moments became short clips. Transcripts were published as crawlable text, extending organic reach and surfacing content on AI-powered discovery platforms long after the event ends. Zoom Clips gave the content team a fast path from raw recording to publishable clip, with no separate editing tool required. Trim, package, and distribute directly from the platform. One well-produced multi-session event, like Marketing Remix, treated as a system, can carry the content calendar for a full quarter. For a repurposing framework that scales, see virtual and hybrid event best practices . What we walked out with Marketing Remix was a deliberate test: could a team plan, run, and extract real pipeline value from a professional multi-session virtual event across five regions without leaving the platform? We came in with a hypothesis. We walked out with a playbook. One platform. Every phase. The engagement signals built throughout, across Q&A activity, poll responses, chat behavior, session duration, and after-party attendance came together at the end into a clear picture of who was ready for the next conversation. What are Zoom Webinars and Events? Zoom Webinars and Events is a virtual event platform that enables organizations to plan, host, and analyze professional virtual events of any size, from single-session webinars to multi-day, multi-track programs with thousands of registrants. The platform includes registration management, branded event hubs, live and simulive session support, real-time engagement tools, and post-event analytics in one environment. For teams running virtual events as a demand generation or community-building channel, a fully integrated platform removes the overhead of managing separate tools for email, production, and reporting. It is available as part of the Zoom Workplace platform, with tiers including Webinars, Webinars Plus, and Zoom Events to match different program scales and production requirements. How do you measure virtual event ROI with Zoom Event analytics? Measuring virtual event ROI starts with moving past registration and attendance counts into behavioral data. The most reliable signals are session duration, Q&A participation, reaction activity, and a composite engagement score that rolls all of those together per attendee. These metrics show who was genuinely engaged versus who opened the tab and walked away, which is the segmentation that helps sales teams prioritize outreach. Cross-event benchmarking adds a second layer by comparing each event's performance against your full history. Connecting that behavioral data directly to CRM pipeline, routing per-attendee topic signals to SDRs rather than a flat CSV, is what turns a virtual event from a brand channel into a revenue motion. What is an engagement score in webinars, and why does it matter? An engagement score in webinars is a composite metric that combines multiple behavioral signals — session duration, Q&A participation, reactions, chat activity — into a single number per attendee, typically scaled 0 to 10. It reflects the quality of attention, not just the fact that someone showed up. For sales teams, it works as a prioritization filter: highest scorers get immediate outreach, mid-range scores get reviewed for topic context before follow-up, and low scorers route into a lighter nurture sequence. It replaces the default of treating every attendee identically regardless of how they actually engaged.

title: Config 2026: New materials, new tools and a more expressive canvas
summary: Push past what you thought was possible with code layers, Figma Motion, shaders, generative plugins and Weave tools, all on the canvas.
body_text: Design is about asking the hard questions. Right now, these questions feel bigger than ever. What’s changing? What’s possible? And what does it even mean to create? Here at Figma, we keep coming back to one simple premise: No tool should limit where an idea can go. This year’s Config announcements are all about limitless expression on the canvas. We’re supporting new materials to express anything you can imagine and introducing new tools to shape and push these materials further than ever: code, motion, shaders, generative plugins and Weave tools, all on the Figma canvas. At past Configs, we’ve talked about AI lowering the floor and raising the ceiling. But while AI has lowered the floor, it has not raised the ceiling. Designers, creatives, builders: You will raise the ceiling. In the months and years ahead, I believe there will be an explosion of creativity, risk-taking and bold expression. Our goal at Figma is to help you design in a totally unbounded way with materials and tools that compose together, and let you riff and play at the speed at which you think. The canvas is more than where your work lives. It’s also where everything connects. Here’s a look at everything we announced at Config 2026. Code on the canvas For years, the design industry has talked about “design versus code,” and tools (including Figma!) have forced a choice. But this is a false debate. Design is a process. Code is material, just like images, vectors and design layers. For a long time, code has lived in single-player environments built for linear thinking. Stated differently: The material was separated from the process. We believe code should be treated like any other design material. So we are introducing code layers in Figma. On the canvas, you can turn any design layer into an interactive code layer with just a single click (or a prompt). You can quickly duplicate a code layer to explore multiple directions side by side, just like you would with a design frame. From there, it works the way the canvas works: You can riff, comment and iterate with all your teammates in the same file. For moments when you want to move from code back into design layers, you can extract design frames into editable design layers. Then, when you’re ready to go back, one click updates the code layer with what has changed. Join the waitlist at figma.com/config-betas for early access when code layers rolls out starting in July. Read more → Code on the Figma canvas With code layers in Figma Design, you can explore multiple directions with code, side by side with your team. Explore options with code layers on the Figma canvas. Bring design to life with Figma Motion Motion designers make things feel alive in ways that are hard to explain, let alone replicate. So many of us have aspired to make this same kind of magic, yet it has felt out of reach. And it often meant moving into other tools. Starting today, you can build with motion directly in Figma. In Figma Design, we’ve added a timeline, including keyframes, presets and much more. You can build motion from scratch, layer it onto existing designs or ask the Figma agent to generate a starting point. I hope you will find Figma Motion powerful, intuitive and a joy to use. If you’re already a motion designer, Figma removes the repetitive work, so you can focus on pushing your creativity further. Because motion is built on Figma’s platform, it can now be a foundational element of your design systems. You can animate a component once, and that motion travels across every screen and every collaborator’s file, the same way fills and typography do. Lastly, Figma Motion is also built to work in code. When you switch to Dev Mode, the full timeline is visible and inspectable: Every timing value, every easing curve, every keyframe is readable without interpretation. You can copy animation code directly in CSS, JSON or framework-ready React. Motion is also MCP-compatible, so you can pass any animated frame directly to a coding agent for implementation. You can also export as MP4, WebM, Animated SVG or GIF, and we're already working on delivering more formats and export types. Read more → Introducing Figma Motion: Your canvas now has a timeline Motion now lives on the canvas—in the same file as your components, your variables, and your team—so your designs can come to life from day one. Animate your designs using the new timeline in Figma Design. Shader fills and effects Shaders have always existed in Figma, powering our canvas rendering behind the scenes. But making shaders can feel intimidating, and they are hard to share with your team. Now you can describe what you want, or use an image as a reference, and the Figma agent will build it for you. An effect transforms what’s already in the layer, and a fill acts as a new material. Because all of this is built with the Figma agent, shader fills and effects are parameterized by default. This allows you to add controls directly on the canvas and shape them in any way you want. What comes back looks and behaves like it was always part of Figma. Parameters are surfaced as controls, stackable with other effects, and ready for seamless conversion to code and popular formats. Interactive shaders are also coming soon, but we’re working to get performance just right. Read more → Figma’s design agent, now with custom tools and greater context Prompting gets you started. Custom tools, real context, and skills take the design agent further—so what ends up on the canvas actually looks like you. Stack shader effects like Gradient map, Riso print and Luminance particles. Generative plugins We’re seeing more and more teams build their own tools, and we think this is awesome! Every designer has unique workflows. Generative plugins make creating all the tools you want possible. To build a generative plugin, just describe the tool you need: the behavior, the controls and the parameters. No local dev environment or plugin API knowledge required. It feels native to the canvas just like any other Figma tool. For both generative plugins and shaders, you can build something for yourself and share it with anyone in your file. Soon, you’ll be able to publish tools to your team, organization or the broader community. Read more → Figma’s design agent, now with custom tools and greater context Prompting gets you started. Custom tools, real context, and skills take the design agent further—so what ends up on the canvas actually looks like you. An image layout generator plugin helps you organize assets. Figma Weave tools Figma Weave tools apply the same approach to visual content, allowing you to build and reuse expressive workflows. And they are now available in the Figma canvas. Some context: Weave is a node-based canvas where you build generative workflows. You can connect models, transform assets, refine outputs and compare approaches. Instead of prompting for a single result, you’re working with model outputs like clay to sculpt a multi-model workflow that allows you to turn whatever is in your head into a visible process you can inspect, iterate on and reuse. Today, you can build workflows in Weave and publish as templates for others to use or remix. Soon, you’ll be able to publish them as tools for your team, organization or community. To get you started, we’ve added a bunch of Weave tools to inspire you. Read more → Connecting Figma and Weave Today, we’re announcing new ways your Weave creative workflows can live alongside your Figma frames. Use the Transfer style Weave tool to apply a style from a source image to a target image. An agent that knows how you work The Figma agent (launched to everyone yesterday!) is built to understand the design canvas. Skills package up your workflows and conventions into reusable instructions for the agent. You can build your own, use skills from your team or pull from the community. Connectors let the agent reach the tools already in your stack—for example, Notion, Slack, Granola, Hex, GitHub, Atlassian and more—and then send updates back. Attachments can bring in research, briefs or any relevant artifact. Agent chats are also now visible to your teammates by default, so you can see what directions others are exploring and build on their thinking. Of course, you can also make chats private when you need to. The agent is also coming to more surfaces, like FigJam and Slides. Join the waitlist for early access at figma.com/config-betas .
